notes.short: Creation groans like a woman in labor
notes.about: Paul speaks of the whole creation as if it felt pain as a person does, groaning like a woman in labor. Birth pains look ahead to a birth, so the picture points to a joyful deliverance to come, when creation shares “the glorious freedom of the children of God.”

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth
figure.means: all creation, pictured as a woman in labor: suffering now, and waiting for a joyful deliverance

notes.evidence: Sanday (Ellicott's Commentary) says the Apostle gives the rest of creation a human sense of pain, and the childbirth picture looks to a joyful delivery. Calvin calls the groaning in travail a most suitable likeness that will bring forth joyful fruit. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a beautiful thought to represent creation as sharing man's miseries and looking to his redemption.
notes.limit: Not every reader takes “the whole creation” as the world of nature: some read it as mankind, whose groaning can then be meant plainly.

cites.quote: In view of the physical evil and misery prevalent in the world, the Apostle attributes a human consciousness of pain to the rest of creation. It groans and travails together, i.e., every member of it in common with its kind. The idea of travailing, as in childbirth, has reference to the future prospect of joyful delivery.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: it hence follows, that they groan like a woman in travail until they shall be delivered. But it is a most suitable similitude; it shows that the groaning of which he speaks will not be in vain and without effect; for it will at length bring forth a joyful and blessed fruit.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: If for man's sake alone the earth was cursed, it cannot surprise us that it should share in his recovery. And if so, to represent it as sympathizing with man's miseries, and as looking forward to his complete redemption as the period of its own emancipation from its present sin-blighted condition, is a beautiful thought
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.about: Verse 9 names the mouth, then the heart, in the order of the words quoted in verse 8. Verse 10 comes back the other way, in the natural order: belief in the heart first, then confession with the mouth.

lines.words: that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,”
and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead,
For with your heart you believe and are justified,
and with your mouth you confess and are saved.

notes.evidence: David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says confession with the mouth is put first in verse 9 only to match the quotation before it, “in your mouth and in your heart,” and that verse 10 places the two in their natural order.
notes.limit: Putting the mouth first in verse 9 follows the quotation; it does not make confession come before faith.

cites.quote: This is put first merely to correspond with the foregoing quotation--"in thy mouth and in thine heart." ... In Rom 10:10 the two things are placed in their natural order.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Side by side: outsiders find God, Israel refuses
notes.about: Paul sets two lines of Isaiah side by side. Those who did not seek God found Him, while to Israel He held out His hands all day long and was refused. The held-out hands show Him pleading with His own people. Paul draws the same contrast in Romans 9:30-31.

sides.label: Called all day long, and refused
sides.words: All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people

sides.who: those who did not seek Me
sides.label: Found God without seeking Him
sides.words: I was found by those who did not seek Me

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes: the held-out hands plead, and while the Gentiles would obey, Israel was disobedient and God was found by others. David Brown (JFB): God is found by those who seem farthest from Him, missed by those who think themselves nearest. Calvin: God turned to the Gentiles because the Jews made a mockery of His favor. Clarke: the Gentiles found the redemption the Jews rejected.
notes.limit: Paul goes straight on: “God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew” (Romans 11:2). The contrast is between two answers to God, not a claim that every Israelite refused Him.

cites.quote: says that while the Gentiles would be obedient, the character of the Jews was, that they were a disobedient and rebellious people. ... This denotes an attitude of entreaty; a willingness and earnest desire to receive them to favor ... God is represented as stretching out his hands in vain; they rejected him, and he was sought and found by others.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: God is often found by those who apparently are the farthest from Him, while He remains undiscovered by those who think themselves the nearest
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A reason is subjoined why God passed over to the Gentiles; it was because he saw that his favor was become a mockery to the Jews.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: I put my salvation in the way of those (the Gentiles) who were not seeking for it, and knew nothing of it: thus, the Gentiles which followed not after righteousness have attained to the law of righteousness, Rom 9:30, and they have found that redemption which the Jews have rejected.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.about: Two words go out in one order and come back in the reverse order: the kindness and severity of God, then severity to those who fell and kindness to you.

lines.words: Take notice, therefore, of the kindness

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Prosapodosis. He says the two words are not taken up in the same order but in reverse, an Epanodos, and sets them out as goodness, severity, severity, goodness (the BSB's kindness and severity). Jebb puts gentleness (the BSB's kindness) at the beginning and at the close, and calls this an epanodos.

cites.quote: Here, the return to the two words is not direct ... but in an Epanodos ... a Goodness. b Severity. b Severity. a Goodness.

notes.short: “Not ashamed” means Paul glories in the gospel
notes.about: Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel. The words say less than he means: far from being ashamed of it, he glories in it, for it is the power of God for salvation. Later he says, “Therefore I exult in Christ Jesus in my service to God” (Romans 15:17).

figure.name: Tapeinosis
figure.words: I am not ashamed of the gospel
figure.means: Paul glories in the gospel and counts it his highest honour to preach it

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Tapeinosis: Paul counts it his highest honour and glory to proclaim the gospel. Bengel says Paul speaks less strongly here and later speaks of glorying (15:17). Barnes says Paul was so far from being ashamed of it that he gloried in it, and Benson that he rather gloried in it.
notes.limit: The words also answer the scorn the gospel met: the world counted it folly, most of all in a great city like Rome. That reading stands beside this one, not against it.

cites.quote: I count it my highest honour and glory to proclaim it, and to suffer for it, while I have full confidence in its power to accomplish all God’s purposes of grace.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He speaks somewhat less forcibly, as in the introduction; afterwards he says, I have whereof I may glory (ch. Romans 15:17).
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/romans/1.htm

cites.quote: He had so firm a conviction of its value and its truth; he had experienced so much of its consolations; and had seen so much of its efficacy; that he was so far from being ashamed of it that he gloried in it as the power of God unto salvation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In whatever contempt that sacred dispensation, and they who publish it, may be held on account of the circumstances and death of its Author, the character of its ministers, and the nature and tendency of its doctrines; I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ But rather glory in it.

notes.short: “Be against us” means do us real harm
notes.about: Here to be against us means to do us real harm. Enemies can still oppose God's people, but while God is for them, none of them can hurt them or overcome them.

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.means: hurt us or overcome us: enemies may oppose, but cannot harm those whom God is for

notes.evidence: Bullinger, under Metonymy, reads it as who can hurt us or bring evil on us: foes can be against us, but to no hurtful effect. Barnes explains it as who can injure or destroy us, since their power to destroy is taken away. Benson asks what real hurt the world or the devil can do us, and Calvin says Paul does not mean that nothing shall oppose us, but promises victory.

cites.quote: “If God be for us, who can be against as?” i.e. , who can hurt us or bring any evils upon us? They can, of course, be “against us,” but not have any hurtful effect.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Who can injure or destroy us? Sinners may be against us, and so may the great enemy of our souls, but their power to destroy us is taken away.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: who can be against us What real hurt can the world, the devil, or all his instruments, do us by all our sufferings from them?
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: He does not, however, mean, that nothing shall oppose us; but he promises a victory over all kinds of enemies.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: A question whose answer is: no one can prevail
notes.about: Paul asks who can be against us, not to learn the answer but to make his point: if God is for us, no power can prevail against us. The questions in verses 33 to 35 are asked the same way.

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.means: no one, since no power can stand against those whom God is for

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse, with the questions of verses 33 to 35, under Erotesis in Affirmative Negation: questions whose answer, supplied by the mind, is an emphatic no. Clarke answers it himself: no cunning, strength or malice can prevail, so those who love God are safe. Calvin calls these words exclamations and says no power under or above the heavens can resist the arm of God.

cites.quote: where the question is put in the affirmative, and the answer to be supplied by the mind is a very emphatic negative. ... “If God be for us, who can be against us?” “Who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect?” “Who is he that condemneth?” “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom 8:31-35 ).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He who is infinitely wise has undertaken to direct us: He who is infinitely powerful has undertaken to protect us: He who is infinitely good has undertaken to save us. What cunning, strength, or malice, can prevail against his wisdom, power, and goodness? None. Therefore we are safe who love God
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: he now breaks out into exclamations, by which he sets forth the magnanimity with which the faithful ought to be furnished when adversities urge them to despond. ... For there is no power either under or above the heavens, which can resist the arm of God.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Two questions whose answer is “No one”
notes.about: Paul takes up the words of Isaiah 40:13 as two questions with only one answer: no one. No one knows the mind of the Lord by his own understanding, and no one has ever advised Him. The questions honor God's wisdom and knowledge and quiet any complaint against His ways.

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.words: Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?
figure.means: No one: no one has known the Lord's mind, and no one has been His adviser

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Romans 11:34-35 under Erotesis in affirmative negation, a question whose unspoken answer is an emphatic no. Bengel answers it: none, but God Himself. Barnes says the verse affirms that no being could teach or counsel God, to hush murmuring. Calvin says Paul checks men from clamoring against God's judgments, as all are too blind to see His purpose by their own understanding.
notes.limit: The questions deny that anyone finds out God's counsel by his own understanding or advises Him. They do not deny that God makes known by His Spirit what He has chosen to reveal.

cites.quote: where the question is put in the affirmative, and the answer to be supplied by the mind is a very emphatic negative. ... “Who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again?” (Rom 11:34-35 ).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Who? i.e. none: but He Himself.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/romans/11.htm

cites.quote: It is designed to express the infinite wisdom and knowledge of God, by affirming that no being could teach him, or counsel him. ... It is also designed to silence all opposition to his plans, and to hush all murmurings.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He begins here to extend as it were his hand to restrain the audacity of men, lest they should clamor against God’s judgments, and this he does by stating two reasons: the first is, that all mortals are too blind to take a view of God’s predestination by their own understanding
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Adam is “a pattern of the One to come”, Christ
notes.about: Paul calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come”, that is, of Christ. Each stands at the head of many: “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). The likeness lies in contrast: one man's trespass brought condemnation, the other's righteousness life (verse 18).

figure.name: Type
figure.words: a pattern of the One to come
figure.means: Adam, whose one sin brought death to all who came from him, pictures Christ, whose one act of righteousness brings justification and life

original.note: In Paul's Greek “pattern” is typos, a type or figure.

notes.evidence: Clarke says Adam was the type or pattern of the Messiah and traces the likeness: as in Adam all die, so in Christ all are made alive. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) finds it in the public part both bore, each a representative man. Calvin says Paul fitly calls Adam the type of Christ, since all are lost through Adam's sin and restored through Christ's righteousness.
notes.limit: The writers do not make Adam's person a picture of Christ in every way: the likeness is in what one man's act brought to many, and in the next verses it is mostly set out as a contrast.

cites.quote: Adam was the figure, τυπος, the type, pattern, or resemblance of him who was to come; i.e. of the Messiah. The correspondence between them appears in the following particulars ... As in Adam all die; so in Christ shall all be made alive
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The point of analogy intended here is plainly the public character which both sustained, neither of the two being regarded in the divine procedure towards men as mere individual men, but both alike as representative men. … Adam is a type of Him who was to come after him in the same public character
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: But in saying that Adam bore a resemblance to Christ, there is nothing incongruous; for some likeness often appears in things wholly contrary. As then we are all lost through Adam’s sin, so we are restored through Christ’s righteousness: hence he calls Adam not inaptly the type of Christ.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: One trespass set against one act of righteousness
notes.about: Paul sets two acts and their results against each other: one trespass brought condemnation for all men, and one act of righteousness brought justification and life. Here he sums up the contrast between Adam and Christ that runs through verses 15 to 19.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life
figure.means: Adam's one trespass, which brought condemnation, set against Christ's one act of righteousness, which brought justification and life

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Antithesis: one offence to condemnation, the righteous act of one to justifying. Barnes says Christ's righteousness stands opposed to Adam's one offence. W. Sanday (Ellicott's commentary), on verse 15, sets one act of trespass against one of obedience. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) sees one righteousness answer one offense, reversing Adam's condemnation.
notes.limit: Writers differ on whether the one act of righteousness means a single righteous act or the whole of Christ's obedience to death. The note claims only that the two acts and their results are set against each other.

cites.quote: “Therefore as through one offence judgment came upon all men to condemnation, even so too, through the righteous act (δικαίωμα, not δικαιοσύνη) of one, the free gift came upon all men unto a justifying

cites.quote: This is properly a summing up, a recapitulation of what had been stated in the previous verses. ... By the righteousness of one - This stands opposed to the one offence of Adam, and must mean, therefore, the holiness, obedience, purity of the Redeemer. ... As the tendency of the one was to involve the race in condemnation, so the tendency of the other was to restore them to acceptance with God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Now comes the statement of the contrast which extends over the next five verses. ... One man, Adam. One Man, Christ. The action. One act of trespass. One act of obedience.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Adam's disobedience set against Christ's obedience
notes.about: Two men's acts are set against each other. Through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners; through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous. Obedience answers disobedience.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous
figure.means: Adam's disobedience, which made the many sinners, set against Christ's obedience, which will make the many righteous

original.note: In Paul's Greek the two words are parakoē, disobedience, and hupakoē, obedience, set here as opposites.

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists the verse under Antithesis: one man's disobedient act, the obedient act of one. Barnes and W. Sanday (Ellicott's commentary) set Christ's obedience against Adam's disobedience. Bengel calls obedience the opposite here. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) sees God repair in Christ the evil Adam did: the race ruined in one is recovered in the other.
notes.limit: Writers differ on whether the obedience is Christ's death or His whole work as Redeemer. The note claims only that the two acts and their results are set against each other.

cites.quote: “For as by one man’s disobedient act many were made sinners, so by the obedient act of one (i.e., His death) shall many be made righteous.”

cites.quote: Obedience. — This term is chosen in contradistinction to the disobedience of Adam.

notes.short: A cry of anguish over the struggle with sin
notes.about: After describing the war with sin within, Paul breaks out in a cry of anguish and longs to be rescued. The next verse answers the cry with thanks: “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.words: What a wretched man I am!
figure.means: grief at the war with sin within, and a longing to be set free from it

notes.evidence: Bullinger calls the verse a true Ecphonesis (exclamation), closing the chapter. Calvin calls it a vehement exclamation, the voice of one panting for help; Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) the cry of an agonized believer longing to shake off his burden; Barnes a lamentation born of the painful conflict; Clarke, who reads it of a man under the law, the groans of a wounded captive.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether Paul speaks as a believer still at war with sin or of a man under the law before he knew Christ.

cites.quote: This is a true Ecphonesis; but, as concluding the whole of the chapter, it is also in that respect a kind of Epiphonema
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He closes his argument with a vehement exclamation, by which he teaches us that we are not only to struggle with our flesh, but also with continual groaning to bewail within ourselves and before God our unhappy condition. ... it is the voice of one panting and almost fainting, because he does not find immediate help, as he longs for.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: it is the cry of a living but agonized believer, weighed down under a burden which is not himself, but which he longs to shake off from his renewed self.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The feeling implied by this lamentation is the result of this painful conflict; and this frequent subjection to sinful propensities. ... In such circumstances, the mind is overwhelmed with wretchedness, and instinctively sighs for relief.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Flesh and Spirit: two minds set side by side
notes.about: Paul sets two kinds of people against each other in one sentence. Those who live by the flesh set their minds on its things; those who live by the Spirit set theirs on the things of the Spirit. Side by side, the two halves can show that a life takes its course from whichever of the two rules it.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit
figure.means: two ways of life set against each other: a mind set on the things of the flesh, and a mind set on the things of the Spirit

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Romans 8:5 under Antithesis, or Contrast. W. Sanday (Ellicott's Commentary) reads verses 5 to 8 as the antithesis of flesh and spirit, verse 5 on what each is set on. Calvin says Paul sets this difference as an argument from opposites; David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says men are under one or the other, and whichever has the mastery shapes their life.

cites.quote: For they that are (or live) after (or according to) flesh (the Old nature) do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are (or live) after (according to) spirit (the New nature) [do mind] the things of the spirit
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: (5-8) Further description of the antithesis between flesh and spirit in regard to (1) their object, Rom 8:5 ; (2) their nature, Rom 8:7-8 ; (3) their end, Rom 8:6 .
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: He introduces this difference between the flesh and the Spirit, not only to confirm, by an argument derived from what is of an opposite character, what he has before mentioned
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Men must be under the predominating influence of one or other of these two principles, and, according as the one or the other has the mastery, will be the complexion of their life, the character of their actions.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Flesh and death set against the Spirit and life
notes.about: The verse sets two ways against each other. A life ruled by the flesh ends in death; putting the deeds of the body to death by the Spirit ends in life. Each half shows up the other: flesh against Spirit, death against life.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live
figure.means: two ways set against each other: a life by the flesh, which ends in death, and sin put to death by the Spirit, which ends in life

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Romans 8:13 under Antithesis, or Contrast. Barnes puts the two halves as a choice: either our sins die or we do, and if they are put to death we are saved. David Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) hears put to death as a play on die, and says Paul tempers the warning by a bright alternative, life for those who by the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body.
notes.limit: The turn from die to put to death is a play on words of its own; this note is on the two halves set against each other.

cites.quote: For if ye live according to flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through spirit (the New nature) do mortify the deeds of the body (i.e., by reckoning that it died with Christ, Rom 6:11), ye will live.

notes.short: “Not a nation”: those God would make His people
notes.about: Moses calls the Gentiles “not a nation,” as if they did not count as a people at all. Yet out of those who were no people God would make a people for Himself by His grace, and so stir Israel to jealousy.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: those who are not a nation
figure.means: the Gentiles, of no account before God, out of whom His grace would make a people for Himself

original.note: In Paul's Greek the words are ouk ethnei, not a nation: a no-nation, a people with no existence as a people.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis (a belittling): ouk ethnos is a non-people, a thing with no existence, as the Gentiles were, from whom grace now takes out a people. Calvin says God raised up a new people from nothing, since without the hope of eternal life men have properly no existence. Benson says the Gentiles, given Israel's privileges, were not God's people and of no account with Him.

cites.quote: οὐκ ἔθνος (ouk ethnos), a non-people. ... a thing which has no existence at all. ... Such were we Gentiles. But through grace, “a people” is now being taken out from among all nations

cites.quote: God formed for himself a nation from that which was not a nation, and raised up from nothing a new people ... Observe, that a foolish nation, and no nation, are the same; for without the hope of eternal life men have properly no existence.

notes.short: A cry of wonder at the depth of God's wisdom
notes.about: Having set out God's plan of mercy for Jews and Gentiles, Paul breaks out in a cry of wonder and praise at God's wisdom and knowledge, deeper than any mind can reach: “How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!”

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.words: O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!
figure.means: wonder, awe and praise at God's wisdom, too deep for man to search out

notes.evidence: Bullinger calls the verse a proper Ecphonesis (exclamation) joined with Thaumasmos, since it voices wonder. Calvin says Paul bursts into an exclamation, overcome by so great a mystery; Barnes that he voices his admiration; Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) that he gives himself to admiring the divine plan; Sanday (Ellicott) that he breaks out in impassioned praise.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether riches, wisdom and knowledge are three things Paul wonders at or the riches are those of God's wisdom and knowledge; the cry of wonder is the same either way.

cites.quote: This is a proper Ecphonesis, except that it expresses wonder and astonishment, so that it is combined with Thaumasmos.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Here first the Apostle bursts into an exclamation, which arose spontaneously from a devout consideration of God’s dealings with the faithful ... being at length overcome by the sublimity of so great a mystery, he could not do otherwise than wonder and exclaim ... I have therefore no doubt but that he extols God’s deep riches of wisdom and knowledge

notes.short: Riches, wisdom, knowledge, then back again
notes.about: Verse 33 names the riches, the wisdom and the knowledge of God. Verses 34 and 35 take them up in reverse: who has known His mind answers to knowledge, who has been His counselor to wisdom, and who has first given to God to riches.

lines.words: O, the depth of the riches
Who has known the mind of the Lord?
Or who has been His counselor?
Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?

notes.evidence: Jebb says the first line proposes the subject, and that riches, wisdom and knowledge are then taken up again in an epanodos, in the inverted order: first knowledge, secondly wisdom, thirdly riches.
notes.limit: The BSB's words can also be read as the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, two things rather than three.

cites.quote: The first line proposes the subject: … Riches, wisdom, and knowledge, are then, in a fine epanodos, enlarged upon in the inverted order; first, knowledge … secondly, wisdom … thirdly, riches
cites.read: the 1820 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/sacredliterature00jebb
